title: Timebox-Corridor Admission and Kernel-Aware Batch Consolidator
creator: Lina Chen
description:
Summary:
We propose a lightweight admission+consolidation policy (Timebox-Corridor) that hedges small, high-frequency prefill requests for a short time window to form higher-quality batches while preserving latency SLOs. The consolidator is kernel-aware: it considers target kernel shapes when deciding whether to merge requests to avoid repeated kernel switches and to maximize KV-cache reuse. Combined with coordinated prefill/decode start scheduling, this reduces tail latency (95/99) and kernel thrashing on heterogeneous model shapes.

Problem statement:
- Small concurrent requests (short-prefill sequences) create many tiny batches that increase per-token overhead and raise 99th percentile latency due to scheduling jitter and kernel startup costs.
- Kernel selection is sensitive to batch shape; naive admission can cause oscillation between kernels (quantization vs full-fp) or suboptimal kernel paths.
- Prefill and decode phases' misalignment prevents KV cache reuse across requests, losing batching gains.

Goals / success metrics:
- Reduce 99th prefill+decode latency by >= 20% on tail-heavy workloads (measured on our e2e replay traces).
- Keep p50 latency within +5% of baseline and throughput change < 5% for steady-state load.
- Decrease kernel-switch events per minute by >30% for mixed-length traffic.
- No customer-facing errors or regressions in output correctness.

Design proposal (high level):
1) Timebox Corridor Admission:
   - On arrival, small requests (<= threshold tokens) enter a lightweight corridor for up to T_ms (timebox). Corridor holds requests for up to T_ms or until corridor fullness triggers earlier flush.
   - Corridor knobs: timebox (T_ms), max corridor capacity (N_slots), and eviction policy (earliest-deadline-first to preserve deadlines).
   - Short timeboxes (4–10 ms) chosen so added latency stays within SLO for interactive endpoints while enabling consolidation.

2) Kernel-Aware Consolidator:
   - Each corridor tracks a preferred kernel fingerprint computed from shapes and quantization hints (sequence length, token counts, model variant).
   - When merging, we prefer consolidations that preserve kernel fingerprint homogeneity. If merging would force a kernel switch, consolidator either: (a) delay merge until compatible requests arrive (up to T_ms) or (b) fall back to a safe generic kernel path if timebox expires.
   - Kernel cost heuristic combines measured kernel startup overhead and estimated per-token runtime for mixed shapes.

3) Prefill/Decode Scheduling Coordination:
   - Introduce a short scheduling handshake between prefill admission and decode orchestrator that groups prefill epochs to maximize KV cache hits.
   - Optionally start speculative decode on a fallback kernel if predicted decode latency > threshold at T_ms expiration (hedging).

4) Tail-Latency Hedging & Speculation:
   - If admission predicts high probability of exceeding the tail SLO (historical trace model), spawn a speculative decode on a lower-cost kernel with the first tokens to reduce 99th latency. Speculation is cancelled if the main path completes earlier.

Implementation notes and interfaces:
- New Admission module (corridor) sits upstream of existing batcher and exposes a lightweight API: admit(request, deadline_hints, kernel_hints) -> admission_ticket.
- Batcher will accept admission_ticket that may include merge_group_id and kernel_fingerprint. The batcher must ensure kernel affinity during kernel selection and expose kernel_switch_counter telemetry.
- Add kernel_fingerprint metadata to request envelope propagated through prefill->decode pipeline.
- Telemetry: corridor_hold_time histogram, merge_rate, kernel_switches_per_min, speculative_decodes_count, speculation_cancel_rate, per-tenant corridor hit/miss.

Rollout plan and experiments:
1) Simulation: offline replays of 3 weeks of production traces with corridor timeboxes {4,6,10}ms and capacity {8,16,32} to find pareto points.
2) Canary: enable corridor for 10% of internal traffic on a dedicated pool for 48h. Measure 95/99, kernel_switch rate, GPU saturation, fairness by tenant.
3) Gradual ramp: 10% -> 30% -> 60% over 2 weeks with kill-switch.
4) A/B: compare with baseline admission under identical load patterns; collect per-route SLOs and user-visible latencies.

Testing & validation:
- Unit tests for corridor eviction, kernel fingerprint equality, admission tickets.
- Integration test: run end-to-end prefill+decode on replay trace asserting tail-latency reduction and no correctness drift.
- Load tests: synthetic spike tests and microbursts to validate corridor does not amplify bursts and to tune backpressure.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Holding requests adds latency for some requests; mitigated by short timeboxes and deadline hints to bypass corridor for strict-latency traffic.
- Speculative decodes increase GPU work; mitigate by limiting speculation rate and cancelling early.
- Kernel-homogeneity constraint may reduce consolidation opportunities in highly heterogeneous traffic; will tune heuristics to avoid starvation.

Observability and dashboards:
- New dashboard: Corridor Health (hold_time p50/p95/p99, merge_rate, queue depth), Kernel Affinity (switch_rate, kernel_latency_by_shape), Speculation dashboard (spec_count, cancellations, tail latency delta).
- Alerting: corridor_hold_time_p99 > 20ms; kernel_switch_rate increase > 50% over baseline; speculation_cancel_rate > 80%.

Deliverables:
- corridor admission implementation + unit tests (PR).
- batcher changes to honor kernel_fingerprint and admission tickets.
- telemetry + dashboards + playbook.
- canary run summary + decision gate document.

acceptance_criteria: Corridor can consolidate small requests with timebox=6ms by default and provide admission tickets to the batcher.
End-to-end e2e replay shows >=20% reduction in 99th prefill+decode latency on tail-heavy trace set with default knobs.
Kernel-switch events per minute reduced by >=30% on mixed-shape load in canary pool.
Telemetry and dashboard surfaces corridor metrics and kernel affinity. Alerts configured and tested.
Speculative decode logic limited to <=5% of requests in canary and validated not to increase average GPU utilization >10%.
No customer-visible correctness regressions; rollout kill-switch works and reverts cleanly.
